tier_reason: README Benchmarks table gives SerialXML 822.085 ns/iter vs Boost.Serialization 7899.305, Cereal 7945.590, pugixml 1585.212 (code public at benchmarks/xml_serialization_benchmarks.cpp, CPU Intel Core 7 240H stated), but no compiler version or flags are stated for the run (only a GCC 16.1 minimum requirement), so it is first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark run. README lists GCC 16.1 as the minimum compiler (the devcontainer image is gcc:16.2.0); CMakePresets 'release-gcc' preset sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (README's install instructions name a nonexistent 'release-gcc-16' preset); CMakeLists adds -freflection with C++26; no explicit -O level in README or CMake files
corrections.caveats: First-party, single-machine, single-run benchmark (100,000 iterations after 1,000 warmup, one steady_clock measurement, no repetitions/variance); compiler version and optimization flags for the run are not stated (only a GCC 16.1 minimum requirement), so it cannot be tier A. README prose claims '8.3x faster than boost_xml', which does not match its own table (7899.305/822.085 = ~9.6x); the 1.9x vs pugixml prose does match. Output formats are not identical: cereal's XMLOutputArchive runs with its default options (indented output) and Boost/cereal/pugixml all build or stream through their own archive/DOM layers, while SerialXML emits a flat string from a compile-time layout. Numbers were published 2026-09-04 and the library code changed afterwards (last commit 2026-09-07). Repo created 2026-07-12, 0 stars, and it depends on GCC 16 C++26 reflection, so adoption and robustness are unproven.

notes: Numbers and ratios in the record check out (9.61x vs Boost, 9.67x vs cereal, derived from page data). I fixed the compiler/flags description (the preset name in the README does not exist in CMakePresets.json) and the caveat that said the repo was created 'days before' the search; it was created 2026-07-12. Metadata matches: MIT, 0 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-07.

tier_reason: README 'Performance snapshot' compares against rapidyaml 0.16.0. The benchmark code is public (tests/compare_chyaml.cpp, tests/compare_rapidyaml.cpp, tests/benchmark_scenarios.hpp, tests/run_comparison.py), and the compiler (MSVC 19.44), flags (Release plus CHYAML_OPTIMIZE_FOR=SPEED, which CMakeLists maps to /O2 /Gy /Gw with IPO) and CPU (Ryzen 9 9950X) are all stated. That meets A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.44, CMake Release config with -DCHYAML_OPTIMIZE_FOR=SPEED (CMakeLists: /O2 /Gy /Gw /utf-8 on the chyaml target, IPO/LTCG on by default; executables /OPT:REF /OPT:ICF)
corrections.claimed_speedup: chyaml's fast 8-byte event tape parses at about 391 MB/s vs 184 MB/s for rapidyaml 0.16.0 building its arena tree: about 2.13x faster with about 13.18x less incremental memory (6.18 MB vs 81.49 MB) on a 4,627,797-byte, 50,000-record input. Across the 8-shape matrix it is 1.16x-2.16x faster per shape (byte-weighted aggregate 1.92x, geometric mean 1.90x) and uses 1.63x-14.55x less memory. Event tape vs DOM tree is not a like-for-like comparison.
corrections.caveats: First-party, self-run benchmark, not independently reproduced. The comparison is not like-for-like: chyaml's event tape (borrowed input, no tree) is compared with rapidyaml building a full tree through parse_in_arena, which also copies the whole input into the arena on every timed iteration. chyaml's own DOM is not compared against rapidyaml, and the author says the structures serve different access patterns. IPO is set on the chyaml library, but the rapidyaml library added via add_subdirectory does not get it (only the rapidyaml_compare executable does). The rapidyaml numbers were measured 2026-08-24 and the code has changed a lot since (the 2026-09-21 rewrite). Nested mappings is the weakest case (1.16x). The baseline is rapidyaml, a known fast YAML library, not a stdlib/default incumbent. Repo created 2026-08-24, 0 stars.

notes: All numbers in the record match the README. rapidyaml v0.16.0 exists (released 2026-07-22). I kept tier A because code, compiler, flags and CPU are all public or stated. I added the event-tape vs DOM-tree and parse_in_arena copy caveats, which make the 2.1x an upper bound for like-for-like use. Metadata matches: MIT, 0 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-21.

tier_reason: The README Performance table compares against pugixml, RapidXML and libxml2. The benchmark code is public (test/bench_LightningXML.cc, a Google Benchmark harness, with competitor versions pinned in CMakeLists: pugixml v1.14, Boost 1.88 RapidXML, libxml2 v2.14.6), and the compiler (Clang 19), flags (-O3/Release) and CPU (Ryzen 9 7950X3D) are stated. That meets A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Leads every workload in the README table. Default (non-normalizing, zero-copy) parser: Flat 3.82 GB/s vs pugixml 1.46 GB/s, RapidXML 199 MB/s (parse_default) / 1.58 GB/s (parse_fastest), libxml2 DOM 178 MB/s; Large (10K users) 3.31 GB/s vs pugixml 311 MB/s, RapidXML fast 340 MB/s, libxml2 DOM 60 MB/s; Attributes 1.91 GB/s vs libxml2 DOM 34 MB/s; Comment-heavy 13.22 GB/s vs pugixml 2.87 GB/s. The fully conforming StrictParser still leads, e.g. Flat 2.67 GB/s and Large 2.43 GB/s.
corrections.caveats: Single-project, first-party benchmark (not independent). The headline column is the default parser, which skips entity expansion, normalization and three well-formedness checks, while pugixml (load_buffer with default options) and libxml2 decode, normalize and copy. The StrictParser column is the like-for-like one and still leads, but by less. RapidXML's 199 MB/s Flat figure is parse_default; parse_fastest reaches 1.58 GB/s. The benchmark executable is built with LTO, but FetchContent dependencies (pugixml, libxml2) are not. The author flags the depth-14 Tree row as allocation-bound and high-variance for the DOM competitors. Very new, low-adoption project (1 star, created 2026-06-09).

notes: All numbers cited in the record appear on the README. I added the StrictParser and RapidXML parse_fastest figures so the claim is not read as like-for-like against normalizing parsers. Metadata matches: MIT, 1 star, not a fork, last default-branch commit 2026-08-14 (Release 1.3.0).
